interactions.summary: A participant reads the continuation of Beatrice's heavenly location and Lucia's rebuke, and Jiang interrupts to stress that the detail about Beatrice sitting beside Rachel matches Paradise without inconsistency.
Jiang explains that Beatrice does not already know Dante's agony because Dante loves her too much to let her see his pain.

The reading shows Virgil's report restoring Dante's courage, Jiang summarizes Beatrice's name as the trigger of trust and self-belief, and a participant asks why Virgil agreed to help in the first place.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Quoted reading followed by Jiang summary and participant question

claims.claim: Jiang takes the mention of Beatrice sitting beside Rachel as another proof that Inferno stays consistent with the Paradise cosmology already discussed in class.
Jiang argues that Dante's love is precisely why Beatrice does not already know his pain: he does not want the beloved to see his agony.
Jiang summarizes the scene by saying that Beatrice's name restores Dante's trust in Virgil and in himself, making his own salvation imaginable again.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang says the beloved is the last to know because love hides pain from the very person who matters most.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you love this person so much you don't want that person to know
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is one of Jiang's strongest psychological compressions in the late lecture.

signature_moments.moment: The quoted passage gives Dante a flower-like straightening and reopening once courage returns.
signature_moments.source_phrase: as little flowers which the chill of night has bent
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is a memorable restorative image for how Beatrice-mediated assurance changes Dante's posture.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Named as the heavenly figure beside whom Beatrice is seated, used by Jiang as a consistency check against Paradiso.
Part of the heavenly relay that conveys Dante's distress and rebukes Beatrice into action.
The beloved whose name restores Dante's courage and whose heavenly position remains consistent across the whole Comedy.

chronology_notes.note: This packet closes the Beatrice-to-Virgil relay and transitions directly into the final question about Virgil's motive for helping Dante.
